opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the thing I most want from an explanation is that it tells you whether the behavior is happening *for the same reason* on a new input as it was on the inputs you understood.

Concretely: suppose you've got a model, and on the training distribution it does something you're happy with. Say it predicts that the camera will show the diamond is still in the vault, and on the training data that prediction is accurate because the diamond actually *is* in the vault. You'd like some account of why the model produces that output, something like "the model is tracking the diamond, and the sensors reflect the diamond's state, and that's why it outputs 'safe.'" That's the explanation.

Then on a new input, the model again says "the diamond is safe." What I want to be able to ask is: does that same explanation still apply here? Or is the output now being produced by some different mechanism, like someone has tampered with the camera, and the model knows the camera will show a diamond even though there isn't one? In both cases the output looks identical. The difference is entirely in *why* the model is saying it.

So I'm not really trying to get a human-legible story of everything the model is doing. That seems really hard, maybe impossible, for big models. What I want is something more like a mechanistic check: here's an explanation that accounts for the behavior on the cases we vetted, and for a new input I can test whether that explanation still covers it or whether something anomalous is going on. That's the thing we've been calling mechanistic anomaly detection.

And the nice feature is you don't need to understand the anomalous mechanism. You just need to notice that the normal reason doesn't apply. That's enough to say "flag this, don't trust this output," and in a lot of the scary cases, like the model deceiving you or a sensor being tampered with, that's exactly the signal you want.

The hard part, and a lot of what we work on, is what an "explanation" even is formally, in a way that's precise enough to check like this. That's where things like heuristic arguments come in: trying to define what it means for some argument to explain why a model has a particular behavior, without requiring a full proof.

r001.rationale: It says to flag a new case as anomalous when the vetted explanation no longer covers the behavior, narrowing anomalies to cases where the normal reason does not apply.

r002.rationale: It explicitly asks whether the same explanation still applies when the model encounters a new input.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing I most want from an explanation is that it should let me predict what the model does in situations I haven't seen yet, and in particular it should let me notice when the model is going to do something different from what I expected. If I have a story like "the model is doing well on this task because it's tracking the actual thing I care about," then that story makes a prediction about what happens on weird inputs, and I want that prediction to actually be good. The failure mode I'm most worried about is that you have an explanation that fits all the training data fine, but there's some other mechanism in there that only kicks in on some rare distribution of inputs, and your explanation just didn't account for it.

So the way I tend to think about it, an explanation isn't really an explanation of the behavior in the abstract, it's an explanation that lets you anticipate the anomalies. If the model has some behavior on new inputs that your explanation doesn't predict, that should jump out as "something is going on here that I didn't understand," rather than being silently absorbed. And that's a pretty demanding standard. It means the explanation has to be about the mechanism and not just a summary of what the model did, because a summary of what the model did on the training distribution tells you nothing about the parts of the model that were never exercised there.

I'd also say I don't think the explanation needs to be human-readable in the sense of someone sitting down and reading a nice story. It could be a pretty formal object. What matters is that it's checkable—that you can look at the model's behavior on a new input and ask, "is this consistent with the explanation we had, or is this a case the explanation doesn't cover?" If you can mechanically do that, then you've gotten most of what I want, because now you have a way of flagging the cases where the model might be doing something you didn't sign up for, and those are exactly the cases where things like deception or distributional shift bite you.

r001.rationale: It says behavior on new inputs that the explanation does not predict should stand out as an anomaly, making deviations identifiable relative to the explanation.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says an explanation should let us predict the model’s behavior in situations not seen before and that those predictions should be accurate.

astra-6.text:
I’d want the explanation to help me predict what the model will do on new inputs. If you tell me, “Here’s why the model did this,” I should be able to use that account to say, “Then in this other situation, it would behave differently,” and check whether that’s true.

You don’t necessarily need to predict every detail of its output. You might care about a particular property, like whether it’s going to be honest. But then you want an explanation that gives you some traction on when that property will hold and when it will break down, including in situations that are different from the ones you’ve already tested. That’s a much stronger standard than having a plausible story about an example you’ve already seen.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes predicting behavior on new inputs, but it does not state that an explanation narrows which cases would count as anomalous.

r002.rationale: It says an explanation should support predictions in situations different from those already tested and help identify when a behavior or property will hold or break down.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d want the explanation to help me predict what the model will do on inputs I haven’t seen yet. If you explain why it made some particular decision, that explanation should have implications for how it would behave if I changed the input, or put it in a different situation. And then I should be able to check those implications.

There’s a question of which new inputs you care about. An explanation might let you predict behavior on inputs drawn from the same distribution, but fail when you move to a new setting. For safety, we’re particularly interested in whether the explanation continues to work in the situations where we’re worried the model might behave badly. So I’d like something that gives us traction on those counterfactuals, rather than just a plausible story about a decision we already observed.

r001.rationale: The response says explanations should support checked predictions about changed inputs and counterfactuals, but does not state that an explanation narrows which cases count as anomalous.

r002.rationale: The response says explanations should help predict behavior on unseen inputs and continue to work in new settings.
